open-question.question: Where does the new shell-callable fold command live, and what is it called in every rendered command, invariant, doc entry, and test: a flag on the open-question tool's remove subcommand that folds and removes in one process (fold-before-remove atomic by construction, but the tool's one-file contract and the invariant built on it change), or a subcommand of a new self-contained tool file for requirements.md beside the three existing tools, chained before remove with && as the task-list tool is chained with its git step (one tool per document, the harmless superset on a failed remove kept)?
open-question.alternative: The fold lives inside the open-question tool as flags on its existing remove subcommand, called in every rendered command, invariant, doc entry, and test as `python3 {{PLUGIN_ROOT}}/tools/open_questions.py remove <MILESTONE_DIR> "<Short Title>" --option "<option>" --decision --section "<Heading>"` with the decision body on standard input as a quoted heredoc. One process folds the decision into requirements.md and removes the block: it validates everything first (the option, the undermined titles, the section target), renders both files in memory, replaces requirements.md first and open_questions.xml second, and writes requirements.md's original bytes back if the second replace fails, as the task-list tool's move does for its two files. No new tool file is added; the tool's "the one file this tool writes" contract and the CLAUDE.md invariant built on it are rewritten to say it also writes requirements.md's Decisions through this flag. Fold-before-remove becomes atomic by construction: a refused option or failed remove leaves requirements.md unchanged, so the run never strands a fold it must stop on, and each answer's section of the batched call is one tool process fewer, with no ordering resting on &&. The 1,270-line XML tool gains a Markdown parser, a second document, and a two-file rollback path, so its one-file contract, its --help description, and the sole-writer invariant all change; the fold can never run without a removal, so any later adoption by the single-question skills or another writer of Decisions is tied to remove's semantics.

The fold lives inside the open-question tool as its own new subcommand, called as `python3 {{PLUGIN_ROOT}}/tools/open_questions.py fold <MILESTONE_DIR> --section "<Heading>"` with the body on standard input, and the batched call chains it before the unchanged remove as `fold … && remove …`, two separate processes. remove stays exactly as it is; the tool's one-file contract and the invariant are rewritten to say it also writes requirements.md through fold, reusing the tool's existing ToolError, read_body, atomic writer, and test fixtures; no new tool file, parity test, or conftest fixture is added. It adds no fourth tool file to copy into three host trees and keeps every fixed command under the one open-question tool prefix the sweep already writes, while remove's contract and tests stay untouched and fold stays callable on its own. It pays the cost of breaking the one-tool-one-document contract without the atomicity that would justify it: fold-before-remove still rides on &&, a remove failing after the fold still leaves the harmless superset the run must stop on, and an XML tool now also parses Markdown.

The fold lives in a new self-contained stdlib-only Python 3.9+ file named for its document, `core/tools/requirements.py`, beside the three existing tools, with fold as its one subcommand for now, called as `python3 {{PLUGIN_ROOT}}/tools/requirements.py fold <MILESTONE_DIR> --section "<Heading>"` with the body on standard input and chained before the unchanged remove as `fold … && remove …`. The file carries its own copies of the stdin reader, error type, atomic writer, and main, imports no sibling (pinned by a parity test like the task-list tool's), and gets its own flat test files and conftest fixture; the open-question tool and its invariant stay unchanged, and the new tool gets its own short CLAUDE.md invariant. It keeps one tool per document exactly as the task-list tool does, leaves the open-question tool's contract, tests, and invariant untouched, and its document-wide name leaves room for later subcommands for other sections of requirements.md without a rename across every rendered command, doc entry, and test. A fourth tool file with duplicated helpers, a parity test, and a new fixture ships into three host trees; fold-before-remove rides on &&, so a remove failing after the fold leaves the harmless superset the batched call must stop on; and the document-wide name promises a broader writer than a sweep-only fold that is not the sole writer of Decisions.

The fold lives in a new self-contained stdlib-only Python 3.9+ file named for the one section it writes, `core/tools/decisions.py`, beside the three existing tools, with fold as its only subcommand, called as `python3 {{PLUGIN_ROOT}}/tools/decisions.py fold <MILESTONE_DIR> --section "<Heading>"` with the body on standard input and chained before the unchanged remove as `fold … && remove …`. Like the requirements-named tool it carries its own helper copies, imports no sibling, gets its own parity test, test files, and fixture, and leaves the open-question tool and its invariant unchanged. It keeps one tool per document's concern and the open-question tool untouched, and its name states exactly the narrow scope the goal sets (a fold into Decisions, used by the sweep only), so no reader of a rendered command or invariant takes it for a general writer of requirements.md. It carries the same fourth-file cost and &&-based fold-before-remove as the requirements-named tool, and if a later milestone gives other sections of requirements.md a tested writer, that needs a second new tool or a rename through every rendered command, doc entry, invariant, and test.

open-question.question: Does the fold command re-parse requirements.md and re-render the whole file in one canonical layout on every write, normalizing the blank lines of every section it did not touch as the task-list tool does, or splice the decision into the one place it lands and leave every other byte of the file as it stands, so a Recommendation-answer: commit diff holds only the folded decision?
open-question.alternative: On every write the fold command parses all of requirements.md into its heading-delimited sections and renders the whole file back in one canonical blank-line layout, the sections it did not touch included (title heading, Goal, Relevant starting state, every Decisions subsection, Out of Scope), discarding drift silently rather than refusing it, as task_list.py renders TASKS_TODO.md and TASKS_DONE.md. It mirrors the task-list tool's settled convention exactly (one parse, one render, drift normalized on the first write rather than checked), so the new tool's writer, its tests, and its invariant read as the same pattern the project already pins, and the seam around an inserted decision never needs special handling because the whole layout is regenerated. Unlike the task files, requirements.md keeps being written by hand after the tool exists (specify-milestone-starting-state, modify-milestone-goal, review-milestone-requirements, and the three single-question skills' Edit-based folds), so any blank-line drift those writers leave is swept into the next Recommendation-answer: commit as noise unrelated to its answer, the per-answer diff no longer holds only the folded decision, and reverting one answer also reverts normalization a later commit may build on; the render must also model the prose-only file closely enough not to alter content (blank lines inside a fenced block in Relevant starting state, the loose bullets of the milestone 44 and 47 shape), a surface no test covers today. In practice the payoff is small: none of the nine requirements.md files of milestones 40 to 48 holds a doubled blank line or a fence, so normalization would rarely fire.

The fold command reads the whole file to locate ## Decisions, but re-renders only the span from the ## Decisions heading to the next ## heading (or the end of the file) in a canonical blank-line layout, the folded decision included, and writes every byte outside that span back exactly as it stood. Every change a fold makes stays inside the one section the sweep owns a write to, so Goal, starting state, and Out of Scope, which other skills write by hand, are never touched, while the Decisions section itself is kept uniform across a run of many folds without the seam logic of a pure splice. It is a middle form with no precedent in either sibling tool, so its section boundary and render rules need their own tests, and a decision folded under one subsection still drags blank-line fixes to other subsections' decisions (written by the Edit-based folds of the single-question skills) into an answer's commit, so the diff can hold more than the folded decision whenever Decisions has drifted.

The fold command reads the whole file only to locate ## Decisions and the target landing point, inserts the decision text there with exactly the blank lines the two seams need (one blank line before and after the inserted block, adding one only where the neighbouring line is not already blank), and writes every other byte of the file back unchanged, normalizing nothing it did not write. Each Recommendation-answer: commit's requirements.md diff is exactly the folded decision, which keeps one commit equal to one answer in the history that revert-then-re-answer relies on, matches the answer core's existing rule that a fold is a targeted edit and never a rewrite of the file, and needs no layout model of a prose file that the hand-writing skills keep editing. It departs from the task-list tool's whole-file render convention, so the two writer tools follow different write rules that the invariants must state separately, and the seam handling (end of file without a trailing blank line, a subsection holding no body yet, a section ending in a bullet list) is fiddly code that a whole-file render gets for free; any existing drift in the file is kept indefinitely.

open-question.question: Does the fold command write the decision body it reads on standard input verbatim as opaque Markdown, so the runner chooses per milestone between a prose paragraph and a bulleted lead-and-text entry as the two recent shapes of the Decisions section show, or does it render one fixed entry form of its own from the body?
open-question.alternative: The fold command treats the body it reads on standard input as opaque Markdown. It writes the body verbatim, with only its leading and trailing blank lines trimmed, and adds no bullet, bold lead, or paragraph wrapping of its own. The runner chooses the entry's shape each time by matching the subsection it lands in: a prose paragraph where the milestone's Decisions use one subsection per decision (milestones 40–43, 45, 46), a `- **Lead.** text` bullet where they use topical subsections of bullets (milestones 44, 47). It follows the sibling tools' convention of writing what they are given and validating nothing of a format whose rules live in procedure prose, the precedent being `move`'s opaque bar. Both shapes the Decisions section actually takes stay available, and folds by the sweep and by the single-question Edit-based skills look the same in any one milestone, because the same runner judgment ("match the live document") governs both. Nothing mechanical enforces a consistent shape. The runner still decides the form on every fold and writes the Markdown syntax itself, so a bullet can land in a prose subsection, or a lead can be malformed, and nobody notices until a review. What the tool refuses in the body (heading lines, for instance) depends on the sibling refusal-set question.

The fold command writes the body verbatim as opaque Markdown, as in the first option. But the sweep's own file prescribes one entry form for every fold it composes, for example one prose paragraph per decision, rather than leaving the runner to match each milestone's live shape. The tool knows no format, and the rule lives in the skill's prose. Every sweep fold has the same predictable shape without adding any format code or rendering tests to the tool. The runner also skips the per-fold judgment of reading which shape the target subsection already uses. In a milestone whose Decisions use bullets, the sweep's folds come out in a different shape from what the single-question skills and earlier entries wrote there, so one section holds mixed shapes. The fixed form is also a prose rule that no check enforces, so it gives no mechanical guarantee over the first option.

The fold command renders one fixed entry form of its own: a prose paragraph built from the body, which is reduced to plain paragraph text (outer blank lines trimmed, with internal line breaks kept or folded as the tool defines). It adds no list marker or bold lead, so it writes the shape that the answer core's "clean prose" instruction and most recent milestones use. The runner supplies only the decision's text and makes no shape choice. Every sweep fold is guaranteed to be the same well-formed shape, matching the majority shape and the answer procedure's wording. The runner can never emit a stray list marker or a broken lead, and the rendering rule is tested once in the suite rather than re-judged on each run. Folds into a bulleted milestone (the shape of milestones 44 and 47) come out as paragraphs among bullets, and the single-question skills' Edit folds may still write bullets in the same section. The tool also gains a format rule whose home would otherwise be procedure prose, which departs from the write-what-you-are-given convention of `task_list.py` and `open_questions.py`.

The fold command renders one fixed entry form of its own: a `- **Lead.** text` bullet. It takes the lead as its own argument and the text on standard input, and it composes the list marker, the bold lead with its full stop, and the spacing itself. The runner supplies a short lead and the decision text for every fold and makes no shape choice. Every sweep fold becomes a uniform, scannable entry with a short handle, the shape of the two most recent bullet milestones. The tool writes the lead's markup correctly every time, in the same way `insert` composes a task's heading from a title argument. Most recent milestones (40–43, 45, 46) record decisions as prose paragraphs, so bullets would be mixed into them. Each call needs an extra lead the runner has to compose, which the lifted line does not supply. And the format rule moves out of procedure prose into the tool, where the single-question skills' Edit folds do not follow it.

The fold command can render both shapes and the runner picks one per call. Given a lead argument, it renders a `- **Lead.** text` bullet. Given none, it renders the body as a prose paragraph. The runner still chooses per milestone by matching the live subsection, but the tool always writes the markup and spacing. The per-milestone choice between the two shapes the section really takes is kept, while the syntax of each shape is tested once in the tool instead of hand-written in every composed call, so a choice the runner makes always comes out well-formed. The tool takes on two rendering paths and their tests for a format whose rules otherwise live in procedure prose. The runner still makes the shape judgment on every fold, so a wrong choice is still possible, and only the syntax is guaranteed.

The fold command chooses the shape itself by inspecting the subsection it lands in. If that subsection's existing entries are `- ` bullets, it renders a `- **Lead.** text` bullet from a lead argument and the body. Otherwise, and for a subsection it creates or finds empty, it renders a prose paragraph. The runner supplies a lead and the text on every call and never judges the shape. Each milestone's Decisions section stays consistent in shape automatically, whichever shape it began with, with no runner judgment and no chance of a mismatched fold. It is the most code of any option, and it relies on a heuristic parse of free prose in a file that no tool, test, or fixture parses today. An empty or newly created subsection gets an arbitrary default shape. A lead must be composed on every call even where it is dropped. And whether a missing subsection is created at all depends on the sibling missing-subsection question.

open-question.question: When the fold command is given a subsection heading that no ### heading under ## Decisions of requirements.md matches, does it create that subsection at the end of ## Decisions and fold the decision into it, or refuse the call with an Error: line and the file unchanged?
open-question.alternative: The fold command treats a heading that matches no ### heading under ## Decisions as a new subsection. It appends the ### heading at the end of ## Decisions, just before the next ## heading, and folds the decision under it. A heading that matches folds into the existing subsection. The call never refuses for an unmatched heading, so the same call shape serves the first decision of a fresh milestone and every later one. It matches the answer core's fold instruction ("in the relevant existing subsection or a new one") with one call shape. A fresh milestone's ## Decisions is created empty by define_milestone.py and is still empty when the sweep usually runs, so each of its first folds is a miss. Under this option those folds land in the batched call with no extra step, no file edit outside the call, and no per-section bookkeeping of which headings exist. A heading the runner meant to reuse but wrote slightly differently (a reworded topic in the milestone-44/47 bulleted shape) silently becomes a second, near-duplicate subsection instead of failing. The only record of that is the Recommendation-answer: commit diff. How much this costs depends on the match rule the command applies (exact, or folded for whitespace and case as task_list.py matches titles).

The fold command folds only into an existing ### subsection under ## Decisions. A heading that matches none is refused with one Error: line on stderr, exit 1, and requirements.md byte-for-byte unchanged. Creating a subsection is never the fold command's job. A runner that needs a new subsection writes it into the file by some other means before the fold that uses it. A mistyped or drifted heading can never fork the section's structure. This is the same stance task_list.py takes when it refuses an insert anchor that names no section instead of guessing, and it keeps the command a narrow writer that adds only decision text. Every milestone starts with an empty ## Decisions, so the sweep's first answer, and any answer opening a new topic, would always be refused. The run would need a separate step to create subsections outside the batched call, the kind of hand-written file edit the 42% ad-hoc python3 str.replace folds came from. How badly a refusal hurts the run depends on how the batched call treats a fold refusal (skip the question or stop the run) and on whether a call may name no subsection at all, both owned by sibling questions.

The fold command takes an explicit marker (for example a --new-subsection flag) saying the call may open a new subsection. With the marker, an unmatched heading is appended as a new ### subsection at the end of ## Decisions, and a matching heading folds into the existing one. Without the marker, an unmatched heading is refused with one Error: line and requirements.md unchanged. The runner writes the marker into a question's section of the batched call when it intends that question's heading to be new, or possibly new because an earlier section of the same call opens it. New subsections stay one call each, so a fresh milestone's first folds still land inside the batched call. A heading the runner meant to match an existing subsection but mistyped is refused instead of quietly forking the section. Each fold call states the runner's intent, so the command can check that intent. The runner has to decide, for every question when composing the call, whether its heading already exists or is opened earlier in the same call. That is one more judgment per section, and a missing marker in a long batch causes a refusal mid-run. The command also gains a flag and a second code path. A refusal's cost to the run depends on how the batched call treats a fold refusal, which a sibling question owns.

open-question.question: Beyond an empty body, what does the fold command refuse with requirements.md left unchanged (a file holding no ## Decisions heading, a body holding a heading line, anything of the body's prose), given that the sibling tools write what they are given and validate nothing of the formats whose rules live in the shared procedures?

Must every fold name a ### subsection under ## Decisions to land in, as both recent shapes of the section use (one subsection per decision, or a few topical ones), or may a call name none and have the decision land directly under ## Decisions after whatever the section already holds?
open-question.alternative: The fold command takes the ### subsection heading as a required argument on every call (argparse exit 2 when it is missing), so every decision lands under a named subsection of ## Decisions; there is no form of the call that names none. Matches the answer core's current fold rule ("in the relevant existing subsection or a new one") and the goal's wording ("folds the decision under its ## Decisions subsection"), and both recent shapes of the section (one subsection per decision in milestones 40–43, 45, 46; a few topical ones in 44 and 47) only ever hold decisions under a ### heading, so a sweep-folded decision never reads differently from an Edit-folded one; a call that forgot its target fails loudly rather than landing somewhere unplanned, as task_list.py's required position group does. The runner must choose or coin a heading for every answer when it composes the batched call, even when the decision is a one-liner with no natural topic; how a heading that matches no existing subsection is handled (created or refused) is the Missing subsection handling question's, and this option's cost depends on that outcome.

The subsection argument is optional; a call naming one lands there, and a call naming none appends the decision at the end of ## Decisions, after whatever the section already holds, subsections included, with no check of what precedes it. The simplest contract for the runner and the tool: the no-subsection path is a plain append before ## Out of Scope with no lookup, so a run whose decisions have no natural grouping never has to invent headings. Markdown has no subsection close, so text appended after an existing ### subsection reads as part of that last subsection: on a section that already holds subsections the decision silently lands in whatever topic happens to come last, mis-filing it in a way no tool or test notices, since nothing parses requirements.md.

The subsection argument is optional; a call naming one lands there, and a call naming none places the decision directly under the ## Decisions heading, after any existing un-subsectioned text and before the section's first ### heading (at the section's end only when it holds no subsection). Gives an un-headed decision a position that is genuinely "directly under ## Decisions" in the rendered document, never swallowed by a topical subsection, while still sparing the runner a heading for decisions that have no natural group. Un-headed decisions accumulate at the top of the section in fold order while headed ones sit below, a third shape of the section that neither recent milestone shape uses; the tool needs a lookup for the first ### heading on the no-subsection path, one more placement rule to test.

The subsection argument is optional, but a call naming none is refused with an Error: line and requirements.md unchanged whenever ## Decisions already holds a ### subsection; on a section with no subsection yet the decision is appended directly under ## Decisions. Keeps the cheap heading-free path for milestones whose Decisions section is flat prose while ruling out the silent mis-filing into the last subsection, so a section is never left half flat and half subsectioned by the sweep. The same call succeeds or fails depending on what earlier answers in the run folded, so a batched call whose first decision named a subsection would see a later heading-free fold refused mid-run, which the call's stop or skip handling (the Fold refusal handling question's) must then absorb; the rule is also a check of the section's structure that the sibling tools, which validate nothing of their formats, carry no precedent for, so it bears on the Fold refusal set question.

The fold command takes no subsection argument at all and always appends the body read on standard input at the end of ## Decisions; a runner that wants a subsection writes the ### heading line as the body's first line, so one-subsection-per-decision is expressed in the body and joining an existing topical subsection is possible only when it is the section's last. The smallest tool surface: one placement rule, no heading matching or folding, and nothing for the Missing subsection handling question to decide, while still producing the one-subsection-per-decision shape that most recent milestones use. The topical shape (milestones 44 and 47, several bullets per ### subsection) cannot be kept except by accident of order, so sweep-folded decisions of a topical milestone come out as new subsections beside the Edit-folded ones; its viability depends on the Fold body form question (verbatim body) and on the Fold refusal set question not refusing a body holding a heading line.

open-question.question: In the batched call, where does each remove --option value come from: written into the call by the runner from the compact view's lifted pick when the call is composed (the snapshot being live for every block whose lift later succeeds, since a cascade strips a block's whole recommendation half or nothing), or taken inside the call from the lift's own print, for instance through an option-only print the lift subcommand would gain?
open-question.alternative: The runner writes each section's remove --option value into the batched call as a literal quoted argument when it composes the call, copied from the pick the compact view lifted for that block. Inside the call nothing derives or checks the option: the section's lift still runs first and its print is held only as the commit body and as the skip test, and remove receives the value the runner wrote. The open-question tool is unchanged. It needs no tool change, no parsing, and no extra process per section, and it keeps the answer core's rule that the option reaches remove as an exact id rather than parsed out of ANSWER. It is also correct by construction for every section whose lift succeeds: a cascade only strips a block's whole recommendation half and never re-picks it, and the embed check guarantees the pick names one of the block's own alternatives, so the compact-view value is still the live pick whenever the lift that gates the section succeeds. The runner re-types every option by hand into a long call, and a copy slip that lands on another valid alternative id of the same block passes remove's check silently, recording one option in the reconciliation while the commit body names another, with nothing in the call to notice. It also ties the option's source to the compact view carrying the pick, which the Compact view command and Compact view block scope questions settle.

The runner writes each section's remove --option value into the call from the compact view's pick, as in the runner-written option, and the section also compares it, inside the call, with the text before the first spaced em dash of its own lift print; a mismatch is treated as a failure before the fold, so that question's section folds and removes nothing. The open-question tool is unchanged. It keeps the option an exact runner-written id while catching the one failure the plain runner-written form cannot, a copy slip onto another valid alternative id, before anything of that question is written. It pays for both sources: the runner still re-types every option, and each section gains a shell prefix comparison on the lift line, which inherits the spaced-em-dash split's blind spot for an option id that itself contains a spaced em dash, so such a block would be refused on a false mismatch. How a mismatch is reported depends on how the call reports skips and stops, which the Stop report print and Fold refusal handling questions own.

The runner writes no option into the call. Each section captures its lift print in one quoted shell value and takes the option inside the call as the text before the first spaced em dash (the whole line when there is none) through a shell parameter expansion, exactly the RECORDED OPTION rule the lift procedure states in prose today, passing that value to remove --option and the whole line as the commit body. The open-question tool is unchanged. One lift process per section supplies both the commit body and the option, so the value comes from the live document at the moment it is used and the runner has nothing to copy; it needs no tool change and adds only one captured value per section, the one-quoted-value case the shell-literal invariant already exempts. It moves into shell the parse of ANSWER that the answer core deliberately avoids by passing the option separately, and it is wrong for an option id holding a spaced em dash, where remove then refuses the call (after the fold, so the run stops) or, if the truncated text happens to be another alternative id, reconciles against the wrong option. Its shell expansion must also be written so every shell the three hosts run parses it alike.

The lift subcommand gains a print of the recommendation's option alone, and each section of the call takes its remove --option value from that print, captured in one quoted shell value, beside the existing full lift whose line stays the commit body. The runner writes no option into the call, and no text is split in shell. The option comes from the live document as the exact id the tool holds, with no parse at all, so an id containing a spaced em dash is carried correctly and no runner copy can drift from the recorded pick; it matches the tool's existing output contract of bare un-escaped values. It changes the open-question tool (a new flag or mode on lift, its help text, and tests under both interpreters), all rendered into three trees, for a print only the sweep uses, and each section runs a second lift process. The flag's shape may overlap whatever print the Compact view command question adds.

No option value travels through the call. The remove subcommand gains a flag that takes the recorded option from the removed block's own recommendation in-process, reconciling the tagged dependents against it exactly as --option does, and each section passes that flag instead of --option; the lift still runs first as the skip test and commit body. The single-question skills keep passing --option as they do. The option can be neither mistyped nor mis-split, because the tool reads it from the same parsed block it removes in the same process, so reconciliation always matches the pick that was recorded and the call carries one fewer value per section. It changes remove's contract and the reconciliation invariant's stated input (the option passed verbatim by the caller) for a flag only the sweep uses, with its own help text and tests across both interpreters and three trees, and it gives remove two ways of naming the recorded option that must stay equivalent.

open-question.question: Is the compact view of the question document (id, question text, lifted pick) one new print of the open-question tool, such as flags on walk or list that print all three per block in one call, or composed in one fixed shell call from the existing list --with-question and one lift per walked id, each written out in full?

Does the compact view the sweep reads cover every open-question block, the recommendation-less ones included with their question text, so the run can see a sibling a decision might moot, or only the blocks walk prints, since the sweep records nothing for a block without a pick?
open-question.alternative: The compact view covers every open-question block in the document: each block walk prints appears with its id, question text, and lifted pick, and every recommendation-less block appears too, with its id and full question text and no pick, so the run's one read shows the whole open set. The run sees every sibling a recorded decision could moot or force, the recommendation-less ones included, which is what the answer core's analyse step asks about and the only basis on which a mooted recommendation-less block can be judged; and it costs little, since after a full recommendation pass the recommendation-less blocks are only the few it skipped, and list --with-question, today's half of the view, already prints every block's id and question text. It carries text the sweep records nothing for, a cost that grows with every block still lacking a pick (a milestone swept part-way through its recommendation pass); and the extra text is used only if the sweep still judges mooting and contradictions per question, so its worth depends on the sibling axes of whether the batched sweep keeps the cascade to mooted entries and where the contradiction advisory is formed.

The compact view covers only the blocks walk prints, each with its id, question text, and lifted pick; recommendation-less blocks appear in it in no form, matching the sweep's rule that it records nothing for a block without a pick and leaves those blocks untouched. The view holds exactly the set the run records and nothing else, the smallest read that still gives each pick its question, and it makes plain in the skill's own reading that recommendation-less blocks are the recommendation pass's and the next review pass's business, never the sweep's. A decision that moots a recommendation-less sibling can no longer be noticed by the run, so that block stays standing until a later review pass tidies it, and any per-question mooting judgment the sweep keeps loses part of its scope; and if the view is composed from the existing list --with-question print rather than from a new tool print (the sibling question on the view's command), that print's recommendation-less lines must be filtered out, adding a step to the fixed call rather than saving one.

The compact view covers every block, but at two degrees of detail: each block walk prints appears with its id, question text, and lifted pick, while each recommendation-less block appears by its id (its Short Title) alone, with no question text and no pick. The run still learns which siblings stand beside the walked set, so a decision that plainly bears on one of them by its handle can be noticed, at a fraction of the cost of carrying every recommendation-less block's full question text. A 2–5 word Short Title is too terse to judge mooting or forcing reliably, so acting on a suspected mooted block needs a further locate the batched call was meant to remove, and the view gains a second line form for the read to distinguish; like the full form, its value depends on the sibling axis of whether the batched sweep keeps the cascade to mooted entries.

open-question.question: Once the sweep writes lift, fold, remove, and commit into its own batched call, does it still follow the two shared answer procedures for anything (the lift step's no-recommendation guard, the answer core's analyse questions), or does its own file state every per-question step and the two procedures say they are followed by the single-question skills alone, as the recommendation pass's batching did in its own file?

Does the batched sweep keep the answer core's cascade to mooted entries, folding an implied constraint and bare-removing the mooted block inside the mooting answer's section of the call, or drop that judgment from the sweep's path and leave an entry a recorded decision moots to the next review pass, given that it fired once in 856 measured answers?
open-question.alternative: Keep the answer core's mooting judgment and cascade in the sweep. The runner forms the judgment before it composes the batched call, once per walked question, against the compact view and requirements.md. When a pick moots another entry or forces its answer, that question's section of the call carries a second fold for the implied constraint and then a bare remove of the mooted block, after the question's own remove and before its commit. Both changes ride in that question's one Recommendation-answer commit. A failure of either cascade step is a failure after a fold, so it stops the run with the tree resumable. If the mooted block is itself walked later, its lift then fails and the run skips it silently. The sweep keeps recording exactly what the single-question skills record. A decision that settles a sibling records the implied constraint at the moment it is made and removes the stale block, so nothing the answer settled stays open for the rest of the run or reaches a later answer. Revert-then-re-answer still restores both blocks with the one commit. The fixed template gains an optional per-section branch: a second fold and a variable number of bare removes. Every run carries it in prose and in testing, yet it fired once in 856 measured answers. The judgment must also be formed before the call runs, from a snapshot that cannot show the effect of earlier cascades. Whether the mooted block is visible at all depends on how the compact view's block scope is settled, and whether the sweep still inherits the cascade from the answer core depends on how its procedure references are settled.

Keep the mooting judgment and cascade, but keep them out of the batched template. The runner forms the judgment before composing the call. When it finds no mooting, the run is the one batched call. When a walked question moots another entry, the run splits at that question: one batched call for the questions before it; that question recorded through the existing per-question answer procedure, with its own fold, remove, cascade fold, bare remove, and commit; then one batched call for the rest of the walk order. The cascade is kept with no change to its behaviour, while the batched template stays one fixed shape with no cascade branch. The rare case pays its extra turns only on the runs where it fires, and the common run keeps the full batching saving. The sweep keeps two recording paths, so its file must describe how to split a run and resume it. That rare path is the one least exercised in the field and most likely to drift. The split also brings back the per-question Edit fold the batching set out to replace, in exactly the runs where the cascade fires. Whether the batched call can be resumed partway depends on how the end-of-run walk and the status-line source are settled.

Keep the mooting judgment but drop the cascade's writes. The runner forms the judgment before composing the call. The batched call has no cascade step and records every walked pick as given, so a mooted block that carries a pick is still recorded. Each mooting pair the judgment finds goes into the report as one advisory line beside the status line. Removing a mooted entry, or folding its implied constraint, is left to the next review pass or to the user. The batched template stays free of a cascade branch and the run stays one call. The rare mooting is still surfaced and not silently lost, so the user learns that a recorded decision settled a sibling without the sweep writing anything it was not given. The run still pays for the judgment on every question, yet acts on none of it. It adds a success-path advisory that the terse-reporting rule has to admit. A mooted block that carries a pick gets recorded anyway, as a separate decision that may duplicate or strain the mooting one, until review or the user reconciles them. The implied constraint is never folded, because review never records a decision.

Drop the mooting judgment and the cascade from the sweep's path entirely. The runner never asks whether a pick moots another entry. The batched call carries only lift, fold, remove with the option, and commit for each walked question. An entry that a recorded decision moots stays in open_questions.xml. If it carries a pick and its lift still succeeds, the run records it as given. Otherwise it waits for the next review pass, which may remove a block that a recorded decision covers, as cleanup, or flag it. This gives the simplest template and setup. The judgment that fired once in 856 answers no longer costs every run a step of reasoning or a branch in the call. Removing a block a decision covers becomes the work of the pass whose role already includes that cleanup, so the sweep stays a pure recorder of picks as given. The sweep stops recording what the single-question skills record. When a mooting does occur, the implied constraint is never folded. A mooted block that carries a pick is recorded as its own decision beside the decision that settled it, which can leave a redundant or conflicting entry in Decisions that only a later review or the user reconciles. This depends on whether the sweep still follows the answer core's analyse step, which is the open question of how its procedure references are settled.

open-question.question: When every fold of a run happens inside one shell call, where is the contradiction advisory formed: once upfront over the whole walked set, against the recorded Decisions and the run's own earlier picks, before the call is composed, or not at all in the sweep, with a contradiction left for the next review pass to notice?

How does the report step learn whether the batched call committed at least one answer, so it can choose between the Recommendations recorded. line and the no-op line: from one fixed marker line the call prints once after its last section, from a marker line printed per landed commit as the recommendation pass's call does, or from something read after the call such as the end-of-run walk?

Does the completeness walk ride inside the batched call after its last section, so a run without a failure costs one call for the loop and the check together, or stay its own call after the batched one, so that it still runs when a section stopped the call?

alternative.id: Walk in call, skipped on stop

open-question.alternative: The completeness `walk` is written into the batched call as its last command, after the last question section. A stop after a fold ends the call before the walk is reached. This matches today's step 4, which runs the walk only "when the gathered order is exhausted". A run without a failure therefore costs one call for the loop and the check together, and a stopped run gets no walk, as it does today. It takes the full turn saving the goal is after: the check costs no turn of its own on the common path. It also leaves the sweep's existing semantics unchanged, because on a stop the walk would print only the stopped question and the ones never reached. Those are anomalies by construction and tell the report nothing it does not already have. The walk's bare ids now share one output stream with the call's other prints, so they need a fixed header or prefix line before the report can tell them apart from a stop or skip line. How that works depends on the format the sibling questions on the stop report and the status-line source settle. The fixed template also grows by one more command that the runner must copy exactly.

The completeness `walk` is written into the batched call as its last command and runs whether or not a question section stopped. A stop does not exit the call. It sets a stopped state that skips every later section, then control falls through to the trailing walk. On a stop, the report treats the walk's print as the list of blocks left standing, not as a completeness anomaly. It is the only form that is still one call on every path, the stopped path included. Every run, stopped or not, ends with a live list of which recommendation-bearing blocks remain. A stopped run's resume point is then visible without a second command. Each section has to test the stopped state, which adds a guard per question to a template written once per walked id, and that is where a copying error is most likely. The report also needs a new rule: on a stop, the walk's ids are the unreached remainder, not anomalies. That gives the advisory two meanings, and the output still needs the header or prefix that the in-call print requires. The sibling questions on the stop report and the status-line source decide that format.

The batched call holds only the question sections. The completeness `walk` stays its own fixed tool call, as step 4 is today, and runs only when the batched call did not stop. On a stop, the stop report replaces the status line and no walk runs. The batched template stays a loop of question sections plus its commits and nothing else. The walk's bare ids keep their own clean print, with no header or prefix needed to separate them from the loop's output. A walk failure also stays visibly distinct from a failure inside the loop. Every successful run pays one more turn, and the run then pays to re-read its conversation context. That is a share of the setup-and-tail cost that this milestone's batching is meant to cut to its fixed-call floor. The extra call also buys nothing that an in-call walk skipped on stop would not give.

The batched call holds only the question sections. The completeness `walk` stays its own fixed tool call after the batched call and runs on every path, including after a section stopped the call. On a stop, its print is reported as the blocks the run left standing, beside the stop report. The batched template stays as simple as it can be, and the walk still runs whatever the call did. A user resuming after a stop sees, from the live document, exactly which recommendation-bearing blocks remain, and the walk's output stays separate from the loop's. Every run pays a second turn, the common no-failure path included. On a stop, the print is the stopped question plus every unreached one, which is anomalous by construction. So the report needs the same two-meaning rule for the advisory that the always-run in-call form needs, and today's sweep does without that rule because it skips the walk on a stop.

The sweep drops the completeness check entirely, in the call and outside it. The run ends with the batched call's own prints, and the completeness-anomaly advisory is retired from the report. The `CLAUDE.md` invariant for the inline sweep is edited, because it names the end-of-run `walk` as the completeness check. It has the lowest cost and the smallest template and report, since nothing is run, parsed, or reported after the loop. A block left unrecorded still carries its pick, so the next sweep run records it, and git shows exactly which answers landed. It removes the only check that the runner composed one section for every walked id. Writing a long fixed call out by hand, once per question, is exactly where a section can be dropped, and without the walk that loss is silent until someone notices a block still standing. It also removes an input that the sibling question on the status-line source lists as one of its options.

open-question.question: On a failure after a fold inside the batched call, how do the stopped question's Short Title and the tool's Error: line reach the report: the call prints one fixed stopped-at line naming the Short Title and lets the tool's stderr pass through beside it, or it captures each step's stderr and prints the Short Title paired with the Error: line as the recommendation pass's call does for a refused block?
open-question.alternative: The call leaves every post-fold step's stderr unredirected, so the tool's own Error: line (or git's message for a refused commit) reaches the runner's output exactly as the tool printed it, and on that failure the section prints one fixed line naming the question, such as "stopped at" a tab and the Short Title, before ending the call. Only the lift's stderr is silenced (2>/dev/null), so a failed lift stays the silent skip. No error text is held in a shell variable; the report step pairs the stopped-at line with the Error: line printed beside it. The smallest addition to the template and to the shell-literal invariant: no captured err value per step, nothing re-printed, and every failure source (the fold command, remove, a cascade remove, git) reaches the report in its own verbatim words with no capture form to get right per step. The Short Title and the Error: line arrive as two separate lines whose pairing the runner must make itself, and stderr and stdout interleave in whatever order the host's tool output merges them; it departs from the paired-line form the recommendation pass's call already uses, so the two batched calls report a failure differently, and the lift's silencing is one more per-step redirect the template must carry correctly.

Each step of a section runs with its stderr captured into one quoted err value (the 2>&1 capture form the recommendation pass's call uses), and on a failure after the fold the call prints the Short Title, a tab, and the captured Error: line as one line, then ends the call; a failed lift's captured text is discarded, which is what keeps that skip silent. Git's refusal of the commit is captured and paired the same way. One self-contained line carries the whole stop report, in the same Short Title-tab-Error: shape the recommendation pass prints for a refused block, so the report step reads it verbatim with no pairing or ordering judgment and the two batched calls share one failure convention a reader already knows. Every step in every section gains a capture wrapper and a printf branch, lengthening a template written once per answered question, and err joins body as a value the shell-literal invariant must exempt; a multi-line git error is folded into the one paired line or split across it, so git's message is no longer shown exactly as printed.

The call prints nothing of its own on a stop: the failing tool's stderr passes through unredirected (the lift's silenced), the call ends, and the report step names the stopped question itself as the next Short Title in the call's section order after the last answer the call reports as landed. The template gains no stop-specific print at all, so the per-section text is shortest and the call's output holds nothing but the tools' and git's own lines plus whatever landed-commit markers the call already prints. It works only if the call's output lets the runner count or name the landed answers, which depends on the axis the Status line source question owns (a single end-of-run marker gives no position); it moves an inference into the runner that a misread count turns into a wrong question named in a stop report, the one report a resume relies on.

open-question.question: When the fold command itself refuses a question's decision, so nothing of that question has been folded yet, does the batched call skip that question and go on to the next section as it does for a failed lift, or stop the run there as it does for a failure after a fold?

Is the batched call's shell template exercised by an automated test that runs the rendered call against a fixture milestone and checks the per-answer commits and the stop path, or verified by the Claude Code hands-on check alone with the other two trees reviewed as rendered, as the recommendation pass's template was?
